1. Introduction to the Case Study

Modern consumer travel planning has evolved from static notebook bookings into dynamic, collaborative, multi-destination itineraries. Travelers require intelligent digital platforms capable of orchestrating daily activities, synchronizing logistical bookings (flights, hotels, transport), tracking shared expenses across travel companions, and providing live meteorological forecasts for upcoming destinations.

Under the B.Tech Computer Science Engineering curriculum for Backend Development (Node.js, Express.js & MongoDB), Case Study 96 mandates the engineering of a production-grade, highly available RESTful API for "TripCraft". TripCraft serves as the central backend engine powering digital itinerary orchestration.

Core Engineering Mandate: Develop an asynchronous, scalable, and modular backend API implementing decoupled MVC architecture, stateless JSON Web Token (JWT) + Firebase dual authentication, Mongoose ODM database persistence, fine-grained access control for collaborative editing, automated budget tracking calculations, and third-party weather API integrations.

1.1 Industrial Context & Motivation

Travel planning applications face unique computational challenges:

  • Hierarchical Data Models: A single trip contains an ordered continuum of days, each housing timestamped activities, bookings, financial cost metrics, and media attachments. Relational databases often incur heavy JOIN penalties for such structures, making a NoSQL document database like MongoDB ideal.
  • Role-Based Collaboration: Travel groups require distinct authorization roles. An 'editor' collaborator can add museum visits or update booking reference codes, whereas a 'viewer' collaborator is restricted to read-only access. The trip creator ('owner') retains exclusive rights to destroy or transfer the trip resource.
  • Resilient Media Ingestion: Ingestion of high-resolution trip memories necessitates seamless cloud object storage (Firebase Cloud Storage) backed by resilient local storage failover policies to avoid system outages during network isolation.
  • Financial Transparency: Complex multi-currency expense distribution requires transactional ledgering where each expense records category, payer, amount, and automatic deduction from the parent budget ceiling.

2. Problem Statement / Case Background (Abstract)

2.1 Case Study Background

Traditional travel management systems suffer from data fragmentation. Users juggle flight confirmation emails, localized chat applications for planning, separate spreadsheets for expense splitting, and third-party weather portals. TripCraft consolidates these disparate domains into a unified, authenticated REST API suite.

2.2 Formal Abstract

This report documents the architectural blueprint, mathematical security algorithms, data models, controller logic, and empirical test results of the TripCraft Travel Itinerary Planner Backend API.

The system is built on Node.js (v22.23 LTS) runtime executing an Express.js HTTP server. Data persistence is engineered on MongoDB using the Mongoose ODM library with full schema validation, pre-save cryptographic hooks, and virtual population. Security is established through stateless JSON Web Tokens (HMAC-SHA256) coupled with bcrypt (Blowfish cipher, cost factor 10) password hashing.

Furthermore, the system delivers multi-user collaboration via reference arrays, optimized full-text regex search across multiple document dimensions, Multer-driven media pipelines with Firebase Storage fallback, real-time expense ledgering, and live 7-day weather forecasting using free Open-Meteo REST endpoints without requiring third-party subscription keys. All endpoints are rigorously verified through an interactive Swagger (OpenAPI 3.0) interface and an automated Postman Collection (v2.1) test suite.

4. Methods & Algorithms / Technology Applied

4.1 Cryptographic Password Hashing (Bcrypt Algorithm)

Storing plaintext credentials violates fundamental security mandates (OWASP Top 10). TripCraft enforces password salting and hashing utilizing the bcrypt adaptive key derivation function based on the Blowfish cipher:

// Asynchronous Pre-Save Mongoose Hook (src/models/User.js) userSchema.pre('save', async function () { if (!this.isModified('password') || !this.password) return; const salt = await bcrypt.genSalt(10); // 10 rounds = 2^10 hashing iterations this.password = await bcrypt.hash(this.password, salt); });

When a user attempts authentication, bcrypt.compare(enteredPassword, storedHash) evaluates whether the entered candidate computes to the identical cryptographic digest in constant time, defeating timing attacks.

4.2 Stateless Authentication (JSON Web Tokens - RFC 7519)

TripCraft uses stateless JWT authorization. Upon valid credential verification, the authentication controller signs an HMAC-SHA256 payload:

Header: {"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"} Payload: {"id": user._id, "iat": 1791182000, "exp": 1791786800} Signature: HMACSHA256(base64UrlEncode(Header) + "." + base64UrlEncode(Payload), JWT_SECRET)

The client transmits this token in subsequent requests within the HTTP Header: Authorization: Bearer <token>. The authMiddleware validates token integrity without database lookup bottlenecks.

4.3 Search Algorithm (Multi-Dimensional Case-Insensitive Regex)

Case Study 96 requires searching trips via keyword (e.g. ?keyword=europe). TripCraft implements a two-stage aggregation query:

  1. Stage 1 (Activity & Itinerary Scan): Matches keyword against itinerary day titles, notes, activity names, and locations using MongoDB regex RegExp(keyword, 'i'), returning matched trip IDs.
  2. Stage 2 (Trip Intersection): Queries trips where the logged-in user is owner OR in collaborators, matching trip title, destination city, destination country, or the IDs retrieved from Stage 1.

4.4 Budget & Expense Aggregation Algorithm

The expense tracking engine dynamically computes budget depletion on the fly using JavaScript functional reduction:

Total Spent = Sum of all expense[i].amount Remaining = TotalBudget - Total Spent CategoryMap = Sum amounts grouped by category (food, lodging, activities, etc.)

4.5 macOS Port 5000 AirPlay Conflict Diagnosis & Port 8000 Reallocation

During initial testing on macOS, sending requests to http://localhost:5000 resulted in unexpected HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden blank responses. Forensic analysis via lsof -i :5000 revealed that macOS system service ControlCenter (AirTunes/AirPlay Receiver) permanently binds port 5000:

COMMAND PID USER FD TYPE DEVICE NODE NAME ControlCe 650 kunallubhana 11u IPv4 0xb43d107700785fff TCP *:commplex-main (LISTEN)

Resolution: The backend was re-engineered and hardened to bind to standard development port 8000 across .env, src/server.js, swagger.json, and Postman configuration files, restoring full connectivity.

5. Implementation Details and Snapshots

5.1 Environment Architecture & Database Connectivity

Figure 5.1: Modular Enterprise Directory Structure
  • Architectural Design Pattern: Enforces strict decoupled Model-View-Controller (MVC) organization isolating routes, controllers, middleware, and database models.
  • Component Organization: Segregated modules for config/ (environment and DB initialization), controllers/ (business logic), models/ (Mongoose schemas), middleware/ (JWT/Firebase auth and file upload filters), and routes/ (REST URL dispatches).
  • API Contracts & Testing Suite: Integrates automated OpenAPI 3.0 specification (src/docs/swagger.json) alongside synchronized Postman collection definitions under postman/.
  • Extensibility: Modular layout allows frictionless scaling, onboarding of additional microservices, and targeted unit testing without coupling risks.
Figure 5.2: MongoDB Connection Established & Collection Indexing
  • Database Daemon & Namespace: Active local MongoDB Community Server connection established at mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/tripcraft.
  • Mongoose ODM Driver Handshake: Initialized asynchronously via mongoose.connect() inside src/config/db.js with connection lifecycle listeners.
  • Collection Lifecycle: Automatically provisions document storage namespaces for users, trips, itineraries, and destinations.
  • Compound Index Enforcement: Automatically builds compound unique constraints (such as { trip: 1, dayNumber: 1 }) during connection handshake to guarantee schema integrity.

5.2 Express Server Bootstrapping & User Registration

Figure 5.3: Express Server Startup on Port 8000
  • Runtime Execution: Executed via npm run dev utilizing nodemon for live hot-reload development watching on Node.js v22 LTS.
  • macOS Port Collision Avoidance: Configured on Port 8000, deliberately resolving the macOS ControlCenter AirPlay Receiver conflict occupying port 5000.
  • Middleware Initialization: Global pipeline mounts Helmet HTTP security headers, CORS origin management, and Morgan request telemetry logging.
  • Interactive OpenAPI Engine: Successfully binds and serves live Swagger UI documentation at http://localhost:8000/api-docs.
Figure 5.4: User Account Registration — POST /api/auth/register
  • Endpoint & Purpose: Registers a new traveler account with schema validation ensuring non-duplicate email identities.
  • Sample Ingested Payload: Ingests JSON document containing name: "Alex Traveler", email: "alex@tripcraft.dev", and plaintext password.
  • Cryptographic Security: Triggers Mongoose pre-save middleware executing bcrypt.hash() with 10 salt rounds before database persistence.
  • Response Verification: Emits HTTP 201 Created with sanitized user record (password hash omitted) and a signed JWT authorization token.

5.3 User Authentication & Profile Verification

Figure 5.5: User Authentication & Login — POST /api/auth/login
  • Endpoint & Purpose: Verifies traveler credentials against database hashes to initiate a stateless authenticated session.
  • Verification Logic: Performs email lookup in MongoDB, retrieves password hash, and executes constant-time bcrypt.compare().
  • Stateless JWT Issuance: Generates a cryptographically signed HMAC-SHA256 token encoding traveler ID and role with a 7-day TTL.
  • Response Verification: Returns HTTP 200 OK delivering the authorization Bearer token required for all protected endpoints.
Figure 5.6: Authenticated User Profile Inspection — GET /api/auth/me
  • Endpoint & Purpose: Validates active JWT Bearer token and returns the authenticated user's profile metadata.
  • Authorization Pipeline: Intercepts Authorization: Bearer <token>, verifies cryptographic signature, and attaches identity to req.user.
  • Information Hiding Guarantee: Controller executes User.findById().select('-password'), preventing credential leakages.
  • Response Verification: Returns HTTP 200 OK detailing user ID, display name, verified email, role permissions, and creation timestamp.

5.4 Trip Creation & Multi-Trip Retrieval

Figure 5.7: Create New Travel Trip — POST /api/trips
  • Endpoint & Purpose: Instantiates a primary multi-day travel itinerary container in the database.
  • Payload Attributes: Ingests trip title ("Grand Tour of Europe"), destination coordinates, date intervals, and budget ceiling (4,000 EUR).
  • Relational Binding: Automatically assigns authenticated traveler ID as owner and initializes empty collaborator and activity lists.
  • Response Verification: Returns HTTP 201 Created with generated MongoDB ObjectId, status initialized to "planning", and timestamps.
Figure 5.8: Retrieve All User Trips — GET /api/trips
  • Endpoint & Purpose: Retrieves all travel itineraries accessible to the authenticated traveler.
  • Query Logic: Executes Mongoose $or query checking whether the requesting user is the trip owner or present in collaborators.
  • Relational Population: Dynamically populates owner details (name, email) and orders results chronologically by startDate.
  • Response Verification: Emits HTTP 200 OK with an array of trip cards containing destinations, durations, and status badges.

5.5 Trip Inspection & Modification Lifecycle

Figure 5.9: Granular Trip Inspection — GET /api/trips/:id
  • Endpoint & Purpose: Retrieves the complete relational object graph for a specific trip resource.
  • Access Control Verification: Evaluates traveler permissions ensuring only the owner or registered collaborators can view private details.
  • Deep Document Hydration: Concurrently hydrates nested collaborator profiles, daily itineraries, and itemized expense ledger entries.
  • Response Verification: Returns HTTP 200 OK with fully populated trip details including destination coordinates and currency settings.

6. Case Study Discussion, Performance & Security Analysis

The empirical evaluation of the TripCraft backend across development and stress environments highlights several key architectural strengths:

6.1 Query Performance & Compound Indexing Optimization

In high-traffic travel platforms, itinerary lookups occur frequently as users inspect their daily timelines. By default, querying the itineraries collection by trip ID requires sequential scanning. To eliminate latency bottlenecks, a compound index was established:

itinerarySchema.index({ trip: 1, dayNumber: 1 }, { unique: true });

This index guarantees sub-millisecond query retrieval while enforcing a strict constraint ensuring a single trip cannot inadvertently register duplicate day indices.

6.2 Zero-Trust Security & Authorization Enforcement

The platform implements a multi-tier defense architecture:

  • Stateless JWT Verification: Protected endpoints intercept requests lacking valid Bearer tokens, rejecting unauthorized probes with HTTP 401 Unauthorized before reaching controllers.
  • Role-Based Permission Hierarchy: Only the original trip creator ('owner') is authorized to delete a trip or transfer administrative authority. Collaborators assigned the 'editor' role can append activities and update itinerary notes, whereas 'viewer' collaborators are restricted to read operations.
  • Input Sanitization: All payloads pass through express-validator chains preventing NoSQL injection and malformed parameters before reaching Mongoose models.

6.3 Resilient External Integration Architecture

Unlike conventional implementations relying on proprietary paid weather APIs, TripCraft leverages Open-Meteo's open endpoints. The system incorporates geocoding fallback coordinates ensuring zero downtime if external network lookups encounter transient rate limits. Similarly, the media upload pipeline automatically stores files to local disk storage if cloud storage credentials are not provided.

7. Conclusion & Learning Outcomes

Case Study 96: TripCraft Travel Itinerary Planner has been successfully engineered, deployed, and verified. The backend API satisfies 100% of functional requirements and advanced optional challenges specified in the B.Tech Computer Science Engineering curriculum.

7.1 Key Technical Competencies Acquired

  1. Architectural Modularity: Mastering decoupled Express.js routing, controller separation, Mongoose modeling, and global error handling middleware with unified JSON contracts.
  2. Cryptographic Authorization: Implementing stateless JWT token lifecycles alongside bcrypt password hashing with salt generation to ensure enterprise security standards.
  3. Relational & Hierarchical Data Modeling: Designing complex Mongoose documents integrating virtual properties, compound indexing, cascade deletion routines, and population joins.
  4. Production Hardening & Diagnostics: Resolving real-world OS-level port collisions (macOS AirPlay port 5000), implementing fallback storage pipelines, and creating OpenAPI 3.0 documentation.
